description: Curated everyday material classes for BabyLM material-world synthetic data.
notes: Use these classes as scaffolding for generation, balancing, and filtering.
Final training exports should contain natural prose only, not this metadata.
Prefer visible everyday material behavior over microscopic mechanisms, niche facts, or precise scientific claims.
Use cautious language during generation: often, usually, can, may.
Classes are behavior-focused, not strict scientific taxonomies. Some materials may fit more than one class depending on context.

core_properties: often heavier than plastic or wood
core_dynamics: rusts or tarnishes depending on type
contrast_notes: unlike rubber or cloth, metal usually does not stretch or drape
unlike glass, metal often dents or bends instead of shattering
metal can feel cold because it conducts heat away from skin quickly
caveats: thin metal foil bends and tears more easily than thick metal
aluminum does not rust red like iron or steel
different metals vary in weight, hardness, and corrosion
bronze behaves like a hard metal in most everyday examples, but it tarnishes and patinates differently from steel or aluminum

contrast_notes: unlike metal, brittle hard solids usually crack or shatter instead of denting
unlike rubber, they do not bend much before breaking
glass can be transparent, while ceramic and porcelain are often opaque
caveats: thick glass can be stronger than thin glass
not all brittle hard solids are transparent
ceramic tile overlaps with both brittle solids and masonry-like surfaces
terracotta is porous fired clay, so it can overlap with pottery, masonry, and soft clay examples depending on context

core_properties: rough or smooth depending on surface
contrast_notes: unlike glass, stone and masonry often chip, scrape, or crumble rather than shatter into thin sharp pieces
unlike wood, masonry does not split along a grain
unlike cloth or rubber, these materials stay rigid under ordinary pressure
caveats: chalk and charcoal are softer and more crumbly than rock or concrete
granite is usually hard and heavy, but thin pieces can still chip or crack
asphalt can soften in strong heat
tile may overlap with ceramic depending on the scenario

core_dynamics: floats or sinks depending on type
contrast_notes: unlike metal, wood can split along its grain
unlike plastic, wood can absorb moisture and warp
unlike paper, thick wood can support weight
caveats: different woods vary in hardness and weight
thin wood bends more than thick wood
some dense woods can sink, while many everyday wood pieces float

contrast_notes: unlike wood, paper and cardboard are usually thin and easy to fold or tear
unlike plastic, paper often absorbs water
cardboard can hold shape better than thin paper but still weakens when wet
caveats: thick cardboard is stronger than tissue or notebook paper
coated paper may resist water briefly
paper can float briefly but becomes soggy when soaked

contrast_notes: unlike wood or metal, textiles usually do not stay rigid by themselves
unlike paper, many textiles can be bent and washed many times
cloth can drape over an object instead of holding a fixed shape
caveats: canvas and denim are stiffer than thin cotton
flannel and satin are surface/texture-specific fabric words; use them when softness, smoothness, or drape is visible
some synthetic fabrics absorb little water
rope can be strong in tension even though it is flexible

contrast_notes: unlike glass, elastic materials usually bend instead of shattering
unlike cloth, rubber often returns toward its original shape after stretching
unlike paper, rubber usually does not soak up water
caveats: thin rubber can tear
old rubber can crack
soft silicone may not support much weight by itself

contrast_notes: plastic can be rigid like a toy block or flexible like a bag
unlike paper, many plastics resist water
unlike metal, plastic often feels lighter and does not conduct heat as quickly
caveats: plastic behavior varies a lot by type and thickness
some plastics are brittle, while others are flexible
thin plastic film tears and wrinkles differently from hard plastic

contrast_notes: unlike wood or metal, foam compresses easily under pressure
unlike cloth, foam has thickness and can cushion impacts
some foams absorb water, while others mostly resist it
caveats: Styrofoam can crumble rather than spring back
sponges absorb water much more than packing foam
memory foam returns to shape slowly

contrast_notes: unlike liquids, moldable solids can often keep a shape after being pressed
unlike rubber, they may stay dented instead of returning to shape
unlike stone or metal, they deform easily under hand pressure
caveats: wax and beeswax soften with warmth more than clay does
jelly is soft and wobbly, but it does not hold a crisp sculpted shape the way clay or putty can
mud changes as it dries
dough can stretch and sag differently from putty
scenario_hooks: beeswax softening in a warm hand

core_dynamics: scratches or chips depending on hardness
contrast_notes: unlike cloth, these solids hold a fixed shape and can transmit light
unlike ordinary glass, gem-like examples are often treated as very hard but still can chip in thin pieces
ice overlaps with transparent solids but changes state when warmed
caveats: diamond and sapphire are not ordinary bulk materials for everyday containers, so prefer small decorative objects, toy gems, panes, or explicitly pretend examples
ice is hard only while frozen and becomes water when warmed
transparent does not always mean colorless; sapphire can be colored while still transmitting light
scenario_hooks: ice cube melting in a hand
clear stone scratching a softer surface

core_properties: takes the shape of a container
has no fixed shape by itself
contrast_notes: unlike solids, liquids take the shape of their container
unlike sand or rice, liquids spread flat and do not form stable piles
thicker liquids like syrup flow more slowly than water
caveats: some liquids are thick and flow slowly
paint can dry into a solid coating
oil and water behave differently when mixed

core_properties: takes the shape of a container
contrast_notes: can pour like a liquid but does not spread flat like water
can pile up because the pieces rub against each other
does not bend or stretch as one connected object
caveats: fine powders behave differently from larger grains
wet flour or sand can clump and hold shape
sugar and salt can dissolve in water
